eva: Heads-up — saw sustained memory growth on rtx-pool-7 while replaying long-context sessions (~50k tokens). Heap+KV pages kept climbing even after requests finished. Attaching quick profiler snapshot below.

sam: Oof. Any idea if it's KV cache residency or allocator churn?

eva: Looks like KV residency. Top of the heap shows a bunch of small page fragments tied to prefix entries. pmap shows lots of anon pages, and /proc/kpageflags hints frequent page faults during eviction. Snippet:```
# top entries by bytes
prefix_fingerprint=0x9a7c size=48KB refs=1 last_used=12s
prefix_fingerprint=0xb1e4 size=32KB refs=1 last_used=3s
...
# vmstat shows majflt spike aligned with eviction churn
```

raj: Interesting. Did this reproduce with the new keying we rolled last week? (we replaced session-salt with tenant-only compact hash)

eva: Yes — the regression lines up after that change. My theory: the compact key eliminated session entropy, causing different sessions that share a prefix to map to the same cache entries -> increased fragmentation and more frequent small rewrites as sessions interleave. Also our eviction policy treats those as distinct entries because we only check prefix fingerprint + tenant; but the backing page layout ends up fragmented.

sam: Can you paste current key derivation? I want to verify assumptions.

eva: Current KEY = sha256(tenant_id || prefix_fingerprint)  (32B) stored in a cuckoo-map -> value points to a page slab and an LRU token. Proposed minimal change: KEY' = sha256(tenant_id || session_short || prefix_fingerprint) where session_short = first 8 bytes of session_id salt. That keeps short key size but reintroduces session isolation. Rationale: reduces cross-session aliasing without full session namespace explosion.

marie: Wouldn't adding session_short blow out cache cardinality? Our memory budget is fixed per-GPU.

eva: Yes some increase in cardinality expected, but telemetry shows most prefixes are re-used within the same session. The problem now is that completely collapsing session dims causes hot prefixes from many sessions to thrash a single page cluster, creating fragmentation. Adding session_short lets hot sessions own compact locality, lowering cross-session eviction rate. We can also make session_short only apply when prefix_age < N to limit long-lived prefixes from exploding.

raj: Another option: change eviction granularity -> coalesce small fragments belonging to same prefix fingerprint before reclaim. That reduces page fragmentation. But that requires allocator changes.

sam: Quick experiments? If we cheat and set soft-ttl for cross-session prefixes to 5s, do we see lower fragmentation?

eva: I ran that locally. Soft-ttl=5s reduced sustained RSS by ~18% in the replay workload, but latency variance increased for cold sessions. Profiling trace: fewer page faults during steady-state but more prefix misses on replays.

marie: So tradeoff: lower fragmentation vs higher cold miss cost. We need to quantify user-visible impact. Can we add a metric: prefix_reuse_by_session ratio and cross_session_evictions per-tenant?

eva: Already instrumented a counter in the canary agent. Early numbers: tenant A has cross_session_evictions ~ 3.7x compared to before key change. prefix_reuse_by_session peaked at 0.72 for long-lived sessions, meaning most reuse is intra-session.

raj: What about batching? Does interleaving batched requests worsen the thrash (different sessions in same batch writing prefix entries)?

eva: Yes — batch interleaving amplifies writes to the same page cluster. Kernel selection unaffected, but throughput dropped ~6% due to eviction stalls during peak. If we bias the batcher to prefer same-session affinity (session-aware batching), the regression largely disappears.

sam: Good datapoint. Short-term mitigation plan?

eva: Proposal: 1) Roll out session_short keying behind flag (per-tenant opt-in). 2) Add session-aware batching heuristic (prefer grouping same session up to X ms). 3) Add telemetry: cross_session_evictions and fragment_bytes_grown. 4) Medium-term: evaluate allocator coalescing for small fragments.

marie: Ops notes: can we do a controlled canary on a low-traffic shard? We should also add a guard that reduces session_short cardinality if free_memory < threshold.

eva: Yep. I added a gate in the patch: session_short applied only when free_pages_pct > 15% else fallback to tenant-only keying. That avoids sudden memory blowouts.

infra-bot: deploy request queued: canary-deploy kv-key-session-short flag to rtx-pool-7 at 2023-10-12T21:00Z by eva — runbook link: https://runbook.internal/kv-session-short-canary

sam: Nice. For the patch text, include the compatibility note: existing persisted mappings still use old key — we need a migration: ensure lookup tries session_key then tenant_key as fallback to avoid cold miss storms.

eva: Patch includes dual-lookup: try KEY' then KEY. Fallback ensures we don't lose cached content. Also added incremental scrub job to compact fragments every 10m when fragmentation metric > thr.

raj: Sounds reasonable. Can we add a small end-to-end test in the runtime suite that simulates interleaved sessions and checks RSS and evictions under flag on/off?

eva: Yep added tests and perf harness. Local runs pass. I'll push the RFC PR shortly.

marie: :thumbsup: schedule the canary and let's collect metrics for 6 hours before wider roll.

sam: Thanks eva — ping in #incidents if anything spikes.

eva: Will do — thanks all.
